blocks.p: Someone had put fresh flowers in the quiet room.

They were not the same flowers as the day before. Those had been white; these were yellow, a small lamp-grown star with a dark eye, and there were more of them, crowded into the same vase. Sol stood looking at them for a long time while Warden Kell checked something on the wall screen. He wondered who had chosen them. He wondered whether the warden who chose them went home afterward to a family, and ate, and slept well.

He had not slept. He had driven up through the ice the evening before with the white form hanging in the corner of his sight, and he had sat in his rooms with it there through the night. Twice he had begun a petition to the diocesan office in Concord, and twice he had deleted it, because it had nothing in it but the word please. Once he had begun a message to Aurelian, and stopped, because he could not think what he would ask him. At the fourth hour the ice had groaned overhead and cracked like a shot, and then he had found himself on his knees beside the bed with his forehead against the blanket, and could not remember kneeling.
In the morning he had told Pell to pack, and to book their passage, and that he would be back by noon.

“He’s declined the sedative,” Kell said, turning from the screen. “That’s his right, so long as he’s calm. He is very calm.” She smiled. “They often are, at the end. It’s the noise, I think. It makes them strange.”
“Will I be in here?”
“If you like, Your Grace. Most bishops prefer the glass. We don’t listen, you understand, and in the room it’s harder not to.”
“I’ll be in here.”
She inclined her head, as if he had chosen a hymn.
The door at the back opened, and Stephen came in.

He came on his own feet. There were two wardens with him, but he was not leaning on them; one walked a little ahead and one a little behind, and he moved between them in the long slow steps the moon demanded, carefully, the way old men in the archival images had climbed stairs. He had his blanket around his shoulders still, and the cloth bag hung from one shoulder on its strap. In the white light his hair was very thin, and his skin had the transparency of paper held up to a lamp. Sol thought he looked older than he had two nights before. It was possible. Every month a year, he had said.
Stephen saw the flowers first, and smiled at them. Then he saw Sol.
“You came,” he said. “I hoped you would.”

“Five minutes, Your Grace,” Kell said gently, “and then we’ll begin.” She went out with the two wardens, and through the long window Sol saw her settle behind the glass beside them with her hands folded, and reach out, and touch the panel that turned off the sound.
Stephen lowered himself onto the edge of the bed. Sol drew the chair close and sat facing him, near enough that their knees almost touched.
“I went down yesterday,” Sol said. “I followed the transport. I saw.”
“I know. It’s in your face.” Stephen looked at him with a tenderness that Sol found almost impossible to bear. “Was it a girl from Concord? Short hair?”
Sol stared at him.

“They talk through the glass sometimes, the ones who come through holding. Nobody listens. I listen.” Stephen’s mouth moved. “She was very frightened, at first. Then she wasn’t. She told me what she remembered, and I told her the rest. Whatever she was saying at the end, Sol, she wasn’t saying it to the wardens.”
“I can petition Concord. I can go to Concord myself. I am a bishop of Life, Stephen, they will have to...”

It was the first time he had said the name. It came out of him without effort, as though his mouth had been waiting a long while to make that shape, and both of them heard it. Stephen closed his eyes for a moment. When he opened them they were wet.
“Say it again sometime,” he said. “Not now. Listen to me. It came down flagged, didn’t it?”
“Yes.”
“Then a petition will only make them look at you. And they mustn’t look at you, Sol. Not closely. Not now.” He glanced, very briefly, at Sol’s left temple, and away. “You know why.”
“It’s a headache.”

“It’s not a headache.” Stephen leaned forward, his elbows on his knees, so that his face was close to Sol’s, and dropped his voice, though no one was listening. “Something is going to happen to you. Soon, I think. I don’t know what it will be. When it comes, don’t be afraid.”
“You said that in the market.”
“I meant it in the market.” He drew the bag around onto his lap. “I need you to carry something.”

“I don’t believe you,” Sol said. It came out of him like a confession. “You know that. I can’t. I’ve tried. I lay awake all night, and I tried. I don’t remember a ship or a rock or a room with blue lights. I don’t remember you.”
“I know.” Stephen’s hands had gone into the mouth of the bag. “You don’t have to believe me to carry it. You only have to not put it down.”
He stood up. He did it slowly, one hand on Sol’s shoulder for balance, and Sol stood with him without thinking, the way you rise when someone older rises.
“Will you let an old man hold on to you?” Stephen said. “For a moment. It isn’t passed by touch, Your Grace. You know the catechism.”
Sol almost laughed. The sound came out of him strange and broken, and Stephen put his arms around him.

He was so light. That was what Sol would remember. Even in Europa’s gravity, where everyone was light, he weighed almost nothing; he was all bone and blanket. His cheek was against Sol’s shoulder and his hair smelled of the holding house’s soap. And between their two bodies, pressed flat against Sol’s chest by the old man’s thin arms, there was something square and hard wrapped in cloth.

“The copy is for reading,” Stephen said into his shoulder, very low. “The other will come apart in your hands. Keep it anyway. I looked for nine years, Sol. I never found another. As far as I know it’s the last one in all the worlds.”
Sol’s hands had come up. He did not decide that they would. They closed over the bundle against his chest, over the cloth and the two shapes inside it, one soft and one hard, and held them there.
“Read the one about the Word first,” Stephen whispered. “Then read all of it.”
He let go and stepped back, and his empty hands fell to his sides.

For a moment Sol stood in the white room with the bundle held against him. He knew exactly what he was holding. He knew the procedure as well as any man alive; he had helped to write it. The effects of the infected were reviewed, and anything written was reclaimed, because the Virus lived in words. That was the whole reason for the bag and the wardens’ hands reaching for it in the market. That was what he had stopped. He’s a patient, not a prisoner. He had kept these books safe himself, all the way from Abundance, without knowing what they were.
He had never broken the church’s procedure. He had never had the slightest wish to.

He opened the front of his outer robe and put the bundle inside, against his shirt, and drew the robe closed over it, and settled the sash, and stood with his arm across his chest as a man stands when his heart troubles him.
Through the glass, Warden Kell was rising from her chair.
“Thank you,” Stephen said, and sat down again on the bed.

They came back in, Kell and the two wardens, bringing the faint green smell of the corridors with them. One of the wardens carried a cup of something warm. She held it out, and Stephen took it in both hands and drank, and thanked her, and gave it back, and she smiled at him with such kindness that Sol had to look away.
“Lie back now,” Kell said. “That’s it. You’ve nothing to be afraid of.”
“I know,” Stephen said.
He lay back. The warden with the cup set it down and took his hand, as the other had taken Nell Ashby’s, and drew a breath, and began to sing. In the beginning was Life, and Life was the light...
“Thank you,” Stephen said gently. “That’s kind. But I have my own, if you don’t mind.”
The warden faltered. She looked at Kell.
And Stephen began, in his tired, cracked voice, to say something that was not a song exactly, though it had a song’s shape. “The Lord is my shepherd,” he said. “I have all that I need.”
Kell’s face did not change. But she said, quite softly, “Your Grace. You may prefer the glass. For your protection.”
“I’ll stay,” Sol said.
“He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul.”

The warden holding his hand had turned her face away. She did not let go of the hand. Sol saw her lips pressed together, and her eyes fixed on the flowers, and he understood that she was trying, with all of her careful training, not to hear. The other warden reached out and touched two fingers to Stephen’s temple.
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.”
The warden kept her fingers there. Her brow creased. She took them away, and put them back, and held them longer.
“Warden?” Kell said.
“It isn’t answering.” The warden looked up, puzzled. “The Halo. It isn’t there. It’s like touching a stone.”

For the first time Kell hesitated. It lasted no more than a breath. Then her face smoothed again, and she said, “It happens. The old ones, sometimes. Their Halos fail. We’ll do it the old way,” and she went to a cabinet in the wall and came back with a small case, and opened it, and Sol saw a needle.
He had seen one in the archival images. He had never seen one in a hand.

“You prepare a table before me,” Stephen said, “in the presence of my enemies.” He did not look at the needle. He was looking at Sol. “Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life.”

The needle went into the back of his hand. Kell did it neatly and gently, the way she did everything, and pressed the plunger slowly, and taped the line down, and the warden holding his other hand held it a little tighter.
“And I will dwell in the house of the Lord,” Stephen said, more slowly now, “forever.”

His eyes left Sol’s face then. They went up, past the wardens, past the white panels of the ceiling, and fixed on something there, and widened, the way they had widened in the market just before he fell, except that this time nothing went out of them. Something came in.
“Oh,” Stephen said. He said it the way a man says it when he steps out of a door and finds the weather is fine. “Oh. Look. It’s open.”
Sol looked up. There was only the ceiling.
“Lord,” Stephen said, and then a name, the name that would not stay, and Sol heard it and felt it slip away again like water through his fingers, “receive my spirit.”
“Your Grace.” Kell had straightened, and her voice was quiet and patient. “The countersign, when you’re ready.”
The form was there in the corner of his sight. It had been there all night. Release from Mercy. HALE, Stephen. Custody: Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. The blank line waited.

He did not decide to sign it. That was the truth, and he would know it later, and it would not help. He had signed with a thought ten thousand times, and the thought came now the way the response came after Remember the Mountain, by itself, out of the deep habit of four hundred years, before anything else in him could rise up and stop it. His name went into the line. The form closed.

Stephen turned his head on the pillow and looked at him. There was no reproach in his face. There was something else, which Sol had seen once before, the night before last, when the old man held his wrist: grief and its opposite, both at once.
Then Stephen looked up again, at whatever he saw there, and said, very clearly, “Father, do not hold this against him.”
He closed his eyes.

His breathing slowed. It went on slowing, long and quiet and deep, until it was only the breathing of a man asleep at the end of a long day, and then it was further apart than that. Sol watched his chest. It rose, and fell. It rose again, much later, a little. It fell.
He waited for it to rise. The room was so quiet he could hear the flowers’ lamp humming in its stand.
It did not rise.
The warden holding his hand looked at the screen on the wall, and nodded, and laid the hand down on the blanket, carefully, as though it might still be woken.
“There,” Kell said softly. “You see, Your Grace? Like sleep.”

It was. That was the worst of it, or the best; Sol could not tell. It looked exactly like sleep. The lines had gone out of the old man’s face, and his mouth was a little open, and he looked like someone who had fallen asleep in the middle of a sentence he meant to finish in the morning.
They drew the sheet up over him. It drifted down slowly in the moon’s gravity, finding his forehead and his nose and his chin, learning the shape of him, taking a long time to lie down.

Kell lifted the cloth bag from the floor where Stephen had set it. She opened it, and looked inside, and tipped it gently over the foot of the bed. A comb fell out, and a clean shirt folded small, and a cup, and a pencil worn down to the length of a finger joint. Nothing else. She turned the bag inside out to be sure, and shook it, and folded it, and laid it with the rest.
“His effects,” she said. “For reclamation. I’ll need your countersign on those as well, I’m afraid. Since you kept them with him.”
The form opened in the corner of his sight. Effects of HALE, Stephen. One bag, cloth, with contents. Reclaimed in full.

Under his robe, against his shirt, the two books pressed flat against his ribs with every breath he took. He could feel the edges of them. He could feel, or thought he could, the warmth still in the cloth where the old man’s arms had held them.
He signed.

It was not the first false thing he had ever put his name to. He understood that now, standing in the quiet room with the flowers and the sheet and the ten thousand closed forms behind him running grey into the dark. But it was the first he had signed knowing it was false.
“Thank you, Your Grace.” Kell touched his arm. “It’s always harder when they’re ours. Go up and rest. There’s nothing more for you to do here.”

He went out through the white corridors and the atrium, past the chapel with its glowing Window, under the great letters cut into the ice. He has wiped away every tear from their eyes. The fountain rose and fell in the forecourt, slow and white. He got into the car and sat with both hands on the controls and did not move for a long time, and nothing came, no tears, nothing at all; only a kind of pressure in his chest, like a word he did not know.
He drove up through the ice.

Pell was waiting in the residence with their cases packed and stacked by the door. He looked up brightly. “Your Grace. The passage is booked; we leave from the port at the fourth hour. Was the Hale matter resolved?”
“Yes,” Sol said.
“I’m so glad.” Pell reached for the satchel at Sol’s side. “Let me take that, Your Grace.”
“I’ll carry it.”
Pell looked at him, at the arm held across his chest. “Are you hurt?”
“No.”
“Of course.” The deacon smiled and lifted the cases instead, and paused at the door, and said, as he had said ten thousand times, “Remember the Mountain, Your Grace.”
“And forget the tears,” Sol answered. The words came by themselves, as they always did.

But he heard them this time. He heard them all the way down the corridor and into the tunnel toward the port, under the sealed blue ice, with the lamps going by overhead one by one. He walked in the long slow strides of the moon, and he held the books against his chest beneath his robe the way an old man had once held a cloth bag in the Bounty Market, as if it were the only thing he had in the worlds.
Behind his left eye, gently, a thumb pressed from inside.
